question: For certain real numbers \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c,\) the polynomial \[g(x) = x^3 + ax^2 + x + 10\] has three distinct roots, and each root of \(g(x)\) is also a root of the polynomial \[ \begin{aligned} f(x) &= x^4 + x^3 \\ &\quad {}+ bx^2 + 100x + c. \end{aligned} \] What is \(f(1)?\)
solution:
The shared roots let us factor \(f\) without finding the roots themselves. By the factor theorem, the three distinct roots of \(g\) supply three different linear factors of \(f\), so \(g\) divides \(f\).

Both polynomials have leading coefficient \(1\), and their degrees differ by one. Thus, for some \(q\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=(x-q)(x^3+ax^2+x+10)\\
&=x^4+(a-q)x^3+(1-aq)x^2+(10-q)x-10q.
\end{aligned}
\]
Comparing the coefficients of \(x\) gives
\[
10-q=100,\qquad q=-90.
\]
Comparing the coefficients of \(x^3\) then gives
\[
a-q=1,\qquad a+90=1,\qquad a=-89.
\]
We can now evaluate using the factored form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1)&=(1+90)(1-89+1+10)\\
&=91(-77)\\
&=\boxed{-7007}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
